hooks.text: Does your commute dictate your mood?
You think walking is better, but the data is mixed.

A dashboard light in a dark parking lot.

reveal.headline: Walking to work may increase leisure time satisfaction.
reveal.body: While walking to work is linked to higher leisure satisfaction and less strain, it is also associated with lower subjective well-being compared to other modes of transport.

explain.headline: The commute impacts your home and your job.
explain.body: Adverse effects of commuting spill over into your home life and your work. Longer commutes are linked to lower subjective well-being and lower job satisfaction, especially for women.

matters.headline: The commute is an invisible drain.
matters.body: That may be why your day feels heavy. The time spent moving between places is not neutral. It changes how you feel about your work and your rest.

example.headline: The glow of a dashboard in the dark.
example.body: You sit in your car. The engine hums. You are between two lives, neither of which feels fully present.

question.headline: Where does your day actually begin?

verdict: The evidence shows that longer commutes generally correlate with lower well-being and job satisfaction, but the impact varies significantly by transport mode and gender.
caveat: The findings are largely based on observational studies and systematic reviews, meaning they show associations rather than proving that commuting causes lower well-being.
caption:
Your commute is not just a transition between places. It is a system that shapes your well-being. 

Research shows that longer commutes are linked to lower job satisfaction and well-being, though the impact varies by transport mode and gender. These findings are based on observational studies and show associations rather than direct causation.
